title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: a hymn made of nothing but names, and the first selection: Sthanu, the steady post

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nataraja explained, Shiva dancing inside a ring of fire, one foot lifted, one foot planted. Where did you catch something that was moving and steady at once? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A contact in your phone is saved as Mom. Your cousin calls the same woman Auntie. Her boss uses her last name. Her oldest friend has a nickname for her that nobody else is allowed to use. One person, and every name catches her from a different side. Hindu tradition does this with the divine, on purpose, and at length. Some hymns are nothing but names, one after another, like beads on a string. Today we open one of them, and we'll take it a few names at a time: the Shiva Sahasranama.
screen: `ONE PERSON, MANY NAMES.` → `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.` → `THE SHIVA SAHASRANAMA.`

segments.voice: Sahasranama is the hymn's own name for itself: the thousand names. Tradition keeps more than one hymn of Shiva's names. Some readers know it from the Mahabharata, the great epic. Others know it from the Puranas, including the Shiva Purana we read a few days ago. We'll start in the Mahabharata, because the setting is lovely. Krishna wants a son. So he travels to the Himalayas, to the hermitage of a sage named Upamanyu, a devotee of Shiva. Upamanyu tells Krishna what Shiva has done for him, and then he hands Krishna a gift that costs nothing: the names. Near the start of that list come a few short words. Sthira, the firm one. Sthanu, the post. Prabhu, the lord. Bhima, the fearsome one. Stay with Sthanu for a moment. It's a plain word. A post, a pillar, a tree stump that doesn't move when the wind blows. It's an odd thing to call a god. And it sits right next to yesterday's picture: the dancer who never stops moving. The names don't argue with each other. They stack. Shiva is the dancer, and Shiva is the post, and a devotee is allowed to hold both. That's how a sahasranama works. No one name is asked to say everything. Each one is a small door, and you go through the doors one at a time. In temple worship, a priest may offer a flower, a leaf or a few grains of rice at each name, so the hymn becomes a slow walk of offerings. Off the temple floor, the same habit is easy to try: someone you love answers to more names than the one you use.
screen: `SAHASRANAMA: THE THOUSAND NAMES.` · `KRISHNA VISITS UPAMANYU.` · `STHANU: THE STEADY POST.` · `EACH NAME A SMALL DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the post for two minutes. Sit, and let your spine rise like a pillar. Let the shoulders drop around it. Thoughts will blow past like wind. You don't have to chase them or stop them. A post doesn't argue with weather. On each out-breath, feel how little needs to move. If you pray, you can say the name Sthanu softly on the out-breath. If not, the word steady works just as well. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. A hymn of Shiva's names, said one at a time, each name a door. Today's name from it: Sthanu, the steady post.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, notice one name someone you love goes by that you never use, and what it shows about them. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva recite his sahasranama at home or in temples, often on Mondays or at Maha Shivaratri; in a temple archana, a priest may offer a flower, leaf or grain of rice at each name.
